## Overview

The Karata, or Khkhiridi, are a small ethnic group from Dagestan in the North Caucasus. They mainly reside in the Akhvakh and Khasavyurt district and primarily speak the Karata language. The Karata language is an Andic language of the Northeast Caucasian language family, spoken in southern Dagestan, Russia by 9,549 Karata in 2020. The Karatas share a close history with the Avars. Their documented folk-culture context includes livestock raising, farming, bartering, terraced cultivation, Sunni Islam, and the use of Avar as their literary language.

## Festivals & rituals

The Karatas are Sunni Muslims. Islam first arrived in the region as early as the 8th century, but locals adopted the religion around the 16th century under the influence of Sufi missionaries.

## Foodways

Historically, the Karatas engaged in raising livestock, farming, and bartering. They raised sheep, horses, and cattle. Because of adverse natural conditions and a lack of cultivable land, they practiced terraced farming. Rye, flax, wheat, potatoes, and vegetables are identified as staple crops.

## Language & religion

Karata, written in the source as *кӏкӏирлӏи*, is an Andic language of the Northeast Caucasian language family. It is traditionally spoken in Karata, Anchix, Tukita, Rachabalda, Lower Inxelo, Mashtada, Archo, Chabakovo, Racitl, and formerly Siux. Speakers use Avar as their literary language. The language has two dialects, Karata and Tukita, which differ slightly in phonetics and morphology but are mutually intelligible. Four subdialects are named: Anchikh, Archi, Ratsitl, and Rachabalda. Karata has 45 consonants and 18 vowels. The Karatas are Sunni Muslims; Islam reached the region as early as the 8th century, while local adoption occurred around the 16th century through Sufi missionaries.
